extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media and communication researchers, comparative media analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Cross-national survey-based framework that identifies and measures the different influences journalists report as shaping their news selection and production decisions; operationalizes these as six measurable dimensions for comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship; Government officials; Politicians; Pressure from politicians; Political parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures direct or indirect political pressures and formal censorship that shape journalists' selection and framing of news; especially salient in authoritarian and transitional regimes where political influence is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Profit expectations; Advertising considerations; Audience research; Owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes market-driven incentives and commercial constraints (advertisers, owners, audience metrics) that affect what journalists and outlets prioritize; varies cross-nationally and helps distinguish clusters of media systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial supervisors (immediate boss); Editorial policy of the news organization; Owners of the news organization; Managerial considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers internal newsroom hierarchy, formal editorial policies and managerial priorities that structure journalists' routines and selection decisions within organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal values and beliefs; Professional ethics and standards; Time limits; Availability of news-gathering resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses journalistic norms, ethics, time/resource constraints and personal-professional orientations that shape reporting choices; reported as relatively universal across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines and conventions of news work; Verification procedures; Press laws and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to routine practices, verification norms and the legal/regulatory environment that govern newsroom workflows and selection processes; procedural and verification routines are among the most cross-nationally stable influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference-Group Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers in the newsroom; Other newsrooms / competitors; Sources; Public relations; Friends, family, acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures social and inter-organizational reference points (competition, peer norms, source pressure, PR) that indirectly shape news selection and framing; tends to be intermediate in cross-national variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal-Democratic Outlets — implicit news-selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience demand relevance; Professional norms (objectivity, ethics); Competitor coverage; Advertiser sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In liberal-democratic media systems journalists and outlets prioritize audience relevance and professional norms; political influence is typically low while professional and economic influences are comparatively higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarized Pluralist Outlets — implicit news-selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Political alignment with owner / outlet politics; Government source access; Party-affiliated framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In polarized pluralist systems selection and framing are shaped by political/partisan alignments of owners and outlets; access to partisan government sources and party-oriented framing are important drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional / Authoritarian Outlets — implicit news-selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: State-permission framing; Self-censorship of sensitive topics; Loyalty to political patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In transitional or authoritarian contexts political control and coercion lead to heavy state influence, self-censorship, and loyalty-driven coverage; professional autonomy tends to be reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cross-national variability when applying news-values frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness criteria and news-values identified in US/UK research generalize only partially across countries; political and economic influences vary substantially so the same event has different chances of selection across nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and practitioners should not assume universal validity of single-country news-value models; account for country-level differences in political/economic influence when comparing news selection or applying newsworthiness heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability for comparative modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Country-level scores on each of the six influence dimensions can be computed and used as covariates in cross-national news-placement or content models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six dimensions are measurable and intended for use as predictors in comparative quantitative analyses to test and predict coverage divergences across media systems; useful for bridging typologies (e.g., Hallin & Mancini) with journalist-reported influences.
